title: What is KOSA?
excerpt: A closer look at the Kids Online Safety Act and the questions it raises about safety, privacy, and speech.
author: Shari Explains
coverAlt: Original cover artwork for What is KOSA?
body:
## What even is KOSA?

KOSA (Kids Online Safety Act) is a bill that aims to establish certain protections from harmful materials for minors on the internet.

The bill establishes a duty of care in order to protect minors from an app’s design features (things that make an app “addictive,” like infinite scrolling, in-app purchases, push notifications, etc.) on a covered platform.

Duty of care: a required protection against harmful content (suicidal ideation, sexual exploitation, promotion of violence).

Covered platform: an “online platform...video game, messaging application, or video streaming service that connects to the internet and that is used, or is reasonably likely to be used by a minor.” Apps that are classified as a “covered platform” include Instagram, TikTok, and Discord.

KOSA was first introduced in February 2022 by senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) shortly after the Facebook hearings in late 2021.

## Some context…

Back in late 2021, former Facebook employee and whistleblower Frances Haugen leaked internal company documents to the public.

In these documents, it is shown that Facebook was made aware of the harmful effects of its product. Harmful content was shown on the platform, leading to violence in developing countries, declining mental health in users, and the mass spread of misinformation on the platform. Facebook was fully aware of the harm that was being caused, but company executives chose to ignore it due to maximize profit.

These documents being leaked led to journalist Jeff Horowitz publishing the “Facebook Files” series in the Wall Street Journal.

This series and intense media scrutiny led to Facebook being called before the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Product Safety, and Data Security.

## The issue with KOSA…

The bill itself is based in extremely broad terms, which could lead to legal risks for covered platforms.

Many civil rights groups have claimed that if KOSA gets passed, citizens’ First Amendment rights would be infringed upon due to the overpolicing of social media platforms.

Laws targeting the content of one’s speech have to pass a judicial test called strict scrutiny. In this test, the government HAS to prove that the law addresses a specific problem in the least restrictive way possible.

Another hot topic issue related to this bill is the comments made by Senator Blackburn, one of the bill’s cosponsors.

Blackburn once stated that “protecting minor children from the transgender in this culture and that influence... [social media] is where children are being indoctrinated.” She is also actively working with the Trump Administration on her own kids’ safety project.

## What happens next?

KOSA passed the house in a 267 - 117 vote. The bill now has a narrow time window for it to be passed due to the upcoming Senate recess in August.

The bill was set to pass back in 2024, but Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson stalled its passing due to concerns of potential free speech violations within KOSA.

Some major revisions have happened, one of them being the removal of the duty of care, leading to intense criticism from some lawmakers.

The new version does not grant state attorney generals to carry out civil suits over content or speech.

While the revised version is seeking to protect state AI laws, Senator Blackburn’s kids project could block/replac some AI laws in certain states.
